audits.mathematicalReason: Classify by area relative to the square: there are eight smallest triangles, each of area one-eighth of the square; four triangles with a full square side as base and the center as apex, each of area one-quarter; and four half-square triangles formed using a diagonal. Thus the total is 4×2 + 4×1 + 4×1 = 16. This is a defensible application of multiplication within classes and addition across disjoint classes. Rotated triangles remain distinct figures.

audits.mathematicalReason: The original prism measures 9 ft by 3 ft by 1 ft, so its surface area is 2(27 + 9 + 3) = 78 ft². Because the one-foot cubic notch passes through the entire one-foot thickness, it removes three exterior unit-square patches: one from the top and one from each broad face. It exposes three unit squares: the notch floor and its two end walls. The change is −3 + 3 = 0 ft². The mapped scopes support prism/cube face-area accounting and square-area calculations; the notched solid itself is not being treated as a rectangular prism.

audits.derivedAnswer: A: 2√3 − 2, under the standard clock-hour interpretation stated in the text.
audits.mathematicalReason: Let the square's half-side be a. Standard consecutive hour rays differ by 30°, so the triangle between 12 and 1 has base a tan 30° = a/√3 and height a. Hence t = a²/(2√3). A quarter-square consists of two such triangles and one corner quadrilateral, so q = a² − 2t. Therefore q/t = 2√3 − 2. Either tangent with special-angle values or the 30° right-triangle property with Pythagoras supplies the needed side ratio. The assessed composite-area scope and supporting triangle/square area scopes fit both alternatives.
limitations: The rendered rays are unevenly spaced and unlabeled, and one passes through the upper-right corner. The literal drawing does not realize the stated standard eight-triangle/four-quadrilateral partition. The result uses the text's conventional 30° hour spacing, not pixel measurements.

The rays carry no hour labels, and one ray ends at the upper-right corner; equal 30° spacing is supplied by the clock-hour interpretation, not established by the rendering.

audits.mathematicalReason: Put AD = x and let H be the midpoint of AD. Since AB = BD, BH is perpendicular to AD. Writing BH = h gives h² + (x/2)² = 25 and h² + (9 − x/2)² = 49. Subtraction yields 81 − 9x = 24, so AD = 19/3 and DC = 8/3, giving AD:DC = 19:8. Alternatively, the cosine law gives cos A = 19/30, and the isosceles altitude gives AD = 2·5 cos A = 19/3. Both optional routes are valid alternatives, and the segment calculations and ratio simplification fit the assessed scopes.

audits.mathematicalReason: Let the inner equilateral triangle have side s. Triangle DEC is a 30°–60°–90° triangle with DE = s, so DC = s/√3. Since ∠FDE = 60° and DE is perpendicular to BC, ∠BDF = 30°. Together with ∠DBF = 60°, triangle BDF is another 30°–60°–90° triangle, giving BD = 2s/√3. Thus BC = √3s. The two equilateral triangles are similar, so their area ratio is (s/(√3s))² = 1/3. Equilateral properties and the squared similarity ratio are directly assessed; the listed angle and right-triangle facts support this method.

audits.mathematicalReason: Folding gives opposite-face pairs (6,4), (2,5), and (1,3). A cube corner contains exactly one face from each opposite pair, so every corner sum is at most max(6,4) + max(2,5) + max(1,3) = 6 + 5 + 3 = 14. The faces 6, 5, and 3 do meet at a corner, attaining the bound. Thus the net scope and the supplied extremal scope's bound-plus-attainment criteria both fit this method.
